| [NOTE-029](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-029.md) v2 | Krauska & Lau 2023, moving away from lexicalism | The authors argue that lemma-based production models encode two lexicalist assumptions: a morphology/syntax split, and a stored meaning–syntax–form "triad". On that basis the models mishandle Inuktitut polysynthesis, separable Vietnamese idiomatic collocations, Hiaki number suppletion and English verb–object idioms. Updating the representations (treelets) is not enough, because the algorithms — separate lexical retrieval and structure building, word-sized increments — also have to change. They sketch an 8-stage non-lexicalist model and derive qualitative aphasia predictions from it. There are no new data and no implementation. | Read |
| [NOTE-040](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-040.md) v2 | Dreyer et al. 2024, ants vs humans on a piano-movers puzzle | On one T-shaped piano-movers puzzle, the CDF of solved attempts against normalized path length shows large ant groups (≈80 carriers, n=28) well ahead of small groups (≈7, n=48) and a 3-run composite single-ant series. An agent-based model with group-size-independent rules reproduces the difference. Human groups of 6–26 barred from talking or gesturing needed more attempted state transitions than single people (−32% relative to the individuals' median; n=48 groups vs 61 individuals), and talking groups were only slightly better (+7%). | [NOTE-052](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-052.md) v2 | Consciousness in AI: indicator properties | The report assumes computational functionalism and takes a "theory-heavy" approach. From it the authors derive 14 indicator properties: RPT-1–2, GWT-1–4, HOT-1–4, AST-1, PP-1 and AE-1–2. The claim for them is only that more of them raises the probability of consciousness. They assess a handful of systems against subsets of the list and conclude that no current system "appears to be a strong candidate". Transformer LLMs have "only a relatively weak case" for any GWT indicator, because a single forward pass has no recurrence or global broadcast. Perceiver arguably has GWT-1, GWT-2 and half of GWT-4 but lacks broadcast. Among the embodied agents, AdA is the likeliest to meet AE-2. Most indicators could be built with standard ML techniques. The abstract's "no current AI systems are conscious" is stronger than anything the body shows. | Read |
| [NOTE-055](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-055.md) v2 | Pilgrim et al. 2025, foundations of collective intelligence | A conceptual framework, with no model, data or derivation. It sets out individual and collective computational resources in four dimensions: sensing ΣI_i, states S_c × ∏S_i, processes F_c + ΣF_i, and actions ∏A_i (Table 1). It then maps the collective's surplus onto familiar mechanisms (aggregation with noise σ_i²/n, distributional beliefs P(H), memory persistence T_c, division of labour). | [NOTE-092](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-092.md) v2 | Quillien — Luck and intentional action | Across three Prolific studies (N = 198, 673, 142; Likert 1–7), judgments that "X happened because the agent wanted X" track intentionality judgments under manipulations of luck. | [NOTE-117](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-117.md) v2 | Drayson — What motivates mental fictionalism? | Drayson argues that Toon's two motivations for mental fictionalism both fail. The negative argument needs "committed to internal, intentional, causal states ⇒ committed to the representational theory of mind" (her Premise 2), which is false because non-representational functionalism (Lewis, Putnam, Loar) supplies such states. And Toon's positive argument, that pretence lets us genuinely assert that a person is in an overall state S that causes their behaviour, gives him a reason to identify S with the belief and so to be a realist rather than a fictionalist. | Read |
| [NOTE-120](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-120.md) v2 | Better to be a pig dissatisfied than a plant satisfied | The paper argues conditionally. Suppose (A1) sentience comes in degrees, (A2) plants may be "quasi-sentient", and (A3) moral status comes in degrees and is fixed by degree of sentience. Then plants may have partial moral status, generating "some" obligations that are "outweighed by animal interests in most cases" (Table 1). Animals keep prima facie priority, so granting plants moral status "does not require" treating eating plants and eating pigs alike. The authors propose assigning plants "a very low value" of moral status until evidence accumulates (p. 13). A1–A3 are assumed, not argued, and A2 rests on a survey of contested plant-behaviour findings. | Read |
| [NOTE-123](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-123.md) v2 | Freeborn — A Model of Understanding in Deep Learning | Freeborn defines "systematic understanding" as four conditions: an internal model, non-memorizing tracking of a property, bridge principles fixed in the deployed pipeline, and derivation by the agent itself. Four small demonstrations (the genus of a torus, Mars's eccentricity e≈0.096 with Kepler's form built in, grokked modular addition mod 113, and Othello-GPT from Li et al.) show it can be met. The Fractured Understanding Hypothesis (§7.5), which the paper argues for but does not test, says the understanding deep networks reach is characteristically symbolically misaligned, non-reductive, locally fractured, proxy-dependent and representationally fragmented. | Read |

| [NOTE-180](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-180.md) v2 | Clark & Chalmers — The Extended Mind | The paper argues from a functionalist parity claim that a process or standing state which would count as cognitive if it happened in the head counts as cognitive when an external resource carries it, provided the resource is actively coupled to the organism here and now. | [NOTE-185](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-185.md) | The moral psychology of obligation | Tomasello proposes that the human sense of obligation is "the internalized social/rational pressure from a joint or collective self-regulating agent 'we'… to do what 'we' expect me to" (§3). It arises first, around age 3, inside joint-commitment collaboration with a partner, and then, from about 3–5 years, toward in-group members through collective identification. It is a "self-conscious motivation" whose coercive force is a threat to one's cooperative identity. The support is a synthesis of developmental and comparative experiments, mostly from his own lab, on WEIRD children versus chimpanzees; the paper runs no new experiment. | Read |
| [NOTE-187](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-187.md) | On the Evolution, Science, and Metaphysics of Consciousness | Veit's reply to five commentaries on *A Philosophy for the Science of Animal Consciousness* (2023). Its main new content is the metaphysics the book left to one paragraph. He says hedonic "feel" is *identical* with a valence system: "a common currency of sharing evaluative information across multiple control systems". The currency metaphor, he says, is "not Cartesian but cybernetic" (p. 10). He keeps the word "qualia", arguing that Cartesians have no "definitional rights" (p. 9), and he insists the pathological complexity thesis (PCT) is compatible with any metaphysics, dualism and panpsychism included (p. 9). Against his other critics, he defends a bottom-up evolutionary method that uses human data (de Weerd); a naturalism that is neither autopoietic nor biopsychist (Sachs); evaluation-first over prediction-first, consciousness as an adaptation, and graded, partial unity (Suzuki); and the link to welfare science (Chincarini). | Read |
| [NOTE-190](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-190.md) | Real Patterns | A pattern is real in some data "if there is a description of the data that is more efficient than the bit map, whether or not anyone can concoct it" (p. 34). This is Chaitin's incompressibility definition of randomness turned around (p. 32). Dennett uses the criterion, with the Game of Life's gliders and eaters as the stepping stone (pp. 37–42), to defend "mild realism" about beliefs. Folk psychology tracks a real, noisy pattern of enormous predictive leverage. Two rival interpretations can be "different, but equally real, patterns" with no deeper fact to settle between them (p. 49). | Read |
